questions.question: What is the prime factorization of \(360\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Break \(360\) into prime factors: \(360=2\times180=2\times2\times90=2\times2\times2\times45=2\times2\times2\times3\times15=2\times2\times2\times3\times3\times5\).

The prime factors are \(2,2,2,3,3,\) and \(5\), which can be expressed using exponents as \(2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\).

questions.question: What is the prime factorization of \(504\)?

Break \(504\) into prime factors: \(504=2\times252=2\times2\times126=2\times2\times2\times63=2\times2\times2\times3\times21=2\times2\times2\times3\times3\times7\).

The prime factors are \(2,2,2,3,3,\) and \(7\), which can be expressed using exponents as \(2^3\cdot3^2\cdot7\).

questions.question: What is the prime factorization of \(882\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Break \(882\) into prime factors: \(882=2\times441=2\times3\times147=2\times3\times3\times49=2\times3\times3\times7\times7\).

The prime factors are \(2,3,3,7,\) and \(7\), which can be expressed using exponents as \(2\cdot3^2\cdot7^2\).

questions.question: If \((12\div m)+3=15\), what is the value of \(m\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Rewrite \((12\div m)\) as \(\dfrac{12}{m}\):

\[\dfrac{12}{m}+3=15\]

Subtract \(3\) from both sides:

\[\dfrac{12}{m}=12\]

Multiply both sides by \(m\):

\[12=12m\]

Solve for \(m\):

\[m=1\]

questions.question: If \((10\div m)+2=22\), what is the value of \(m\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Rewrite \((10\div m)\) as \(\dfrac{10}{m}\):

\[\dfrac{10}{m}+2=22\]

Subtract \(2\) from both sides:

\[\dfrac{10}{m}=20\]

Multiply both sides by \(m\):

\[10=20m\]

Solve for \(m\):

\[m=\dfrac{10}{20}=\dfrac{1}{2}\]

questions.question: If \((6\div m)+5=17\), what is the value of \(m\)?

solution.exhibit_text:

\[\dfrac{6}{m}+5=17\]

Subtract \(5\) from both sides:

\[\dfrac{6}{m}=12\]

Multiply both sides by \(m\):

\[6=12m\]

Solve for \(m\):

\[m=\dfrac{6}{12}=\dfrac{1}{2}\]

questions.question: A person buys a used truck with a down payment of $\(1{,}500\) and makes monthly payments of $\(320\) for \(2\) years. What is the total amount the person pays for the truck?

solution.exhibit_text:
There are \(12\) months in a year, so \(2\) years is \(24\) months. Determine the total monthly payments:

\[320\times24=7{,}680\]

Add the down payment:

\[7{,}680+1{,}500=9{,}180\]

The total cost of the truck is \(\$9{,}180\).

questions.question: Jake read \(n\) pages for his science homework. Mia read twice as many pages as Jake. Together, Jake and Mia read \(8\) more pages than Sam read. Which expression shows how many pages Sam read, in terms of \(n\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Let \(n\) represent the number of pages Jake read. Mia read twice as many: \(2n\). Together, Jake and Mia read \(n+2n=3n\) pages.

Sam read \(8\) fewer pages than their combined total, so subtract \(8\):

Sam's pages \(=3n-8\).

Zoe read \(15\) fewer pages than their combined total, so subtract \(15\):

Zoe's pages \(=5n-15\).

questions.question:
A survey found that \(0.6\) of the students prefer indoor recess. Which fractions are equivalent to the decimal \(0.6\)?
Select the **four** correct answers.

solution.exhibit_text:
Check each fraction against \(0.6\).

\(\dfrac{3}{5}\to3\div5=0.6\) — matches.
\(\dfrac{6}{10}\to6\div10=0.6\) — matches.
\(\dfrac{60}{100}\to60\div100=0.6\) — matches.
\(\dfrac{2}{3}\to2\div3\approx0.667\) — does not match.
\(\dfrac{9}{15}\to9\div15=0.6\) — matches.
\(\dfrac{5}{8}\to5\div8=0.625\) — does not match.

questions.question: Devon rides his skateboard to the park at a constant speed of \(20\) miles per hour. If the distance to the park is \(5\) miles, how many **minutes** will it take Devon to get there?

solution.exhibit_text:
Devon's rate is \(20\) miles per hour, or \(\dfrac{20\text{ miles}}{60\text{ minutes}}=\dfrac{1\text{ mile}}{3\text{ minutes}}\).

So it takes \(3\) minutes per mile. For \(5\) miles: \(5\times3=15\) minutes.

questions.question: Priya walks to the library at a constant speed of \(10\) miles per hour. If the distance to the library is \(4\) miles, how many **minutes** will it take Priya to get there?

solution.exhibit_text:
Priya's rate is \(10\) miles per hour, or \(\dfrac{10\text{ miles}}{60\text{ minutes}}=\dfrac{1\text{ mile}}{6\text{ minutes}}\).

So it takes \(6\) minutes per mile. For \(4\) miles: \(4\times6=24\) minutes.

questions.question: Carlos jogs to the gym at a constant speed of \(18\) miles per hour. If the distance to the gym is \(6\) miles, how many **minutes** will it take Carlos to get there?

solution.exhibit_text:
Carlos's rate is \(18\) miles per hour, or \(\dfrac{18\text{ miles}}{60\text{ minutes}}=\dfrac{3\text{ miles}}{10\text{ minutes}}\), or \(\dfrac{1\text{ mile}}{10/3\text{ minutes}}\).

For \(6\) miles: \(6\div\dfrac{18}{60}=6\times\dfrac{60}{18}=20\) minutes.

questions.question: Marcus has \(4\) stamp albums with \(432\) stamps in each album. If he transfers his stamp collection to \(5\) albums, each holding \(288\) stamps, how many stamps will be left over?

solution.exhibit_text:
Total stamps in \(4\) albums of \(432\): \(4\times432=1{,}728\).

Total capacity of \(5\) albums of \(288\): \(5\times288=1{,}440\).

Stamps left over: \(1{,}728-1{,}440=288\).

questions.question: Sophie has \(6\) coin albums with \(504\) coins in each album. If she transfers her coin collection to \(7\) albums, each holding \(378\) coins, how many coins will be left over?

solution.exhibit_text:
Total coins in \(6\) albums of \(504\): \(6\times504=3{,}024\).

Total capacity of \(7\) albums of \(378\): \(7\times378=2{,}646\).

Coins left over: \(3{,}024-2{,}646=378\).

questions.question: Diego has \(3\) card albums with \(660\) cards in each album. If he transfers his card collection to \(4\) albums, each holding \(450\) cards, how many cards will be left over?

solution.exhibit_text:
Total cards in \(3\) albums of \(660\): \(3\times660=1{,}980\).

Total capacity of \(4\) albums of \(450\): \(4\times450=1{,}800\).

Cards left over: \(1{,}980-1{,}800=180\).

questions.question:
A spinner is divided into \(5\) equal sections: \(3\) sections are labeled \(2\) and \(2\) sections are labeled \(7\). One side of a fair coin is heads, and the other side is tails. The spinner is spun one time, and the coin is flipped. What is the probability that the spinner lands on \(2\) and the coin lands on tails?

Select the place on the number line that represents the probability.

solution.exhibit_text:
The probability the spinner lands on \(2\) is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) (3 of the 5 sections). The probability the coin lands on tails is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Multiply the two probabilities:

\[\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{3}{10}=0.3\]

Multiply the two probabilities:

\[\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{2}{10}=0.2\]

A grocery store sells \(1\)-gallon containers of milk for $\(4.49\). The store also sells orange juice in an \(8\)-pack of \(6\)-fluid-ounce bottles for $\(2.39\). Suppose the store wants to sell its orange juice in gallon containers instead. To the nearest dollar, how much more would a gallon of orange juice cost than a gallon of milk?

Enter your answer in the space.

solution.exhibit_text:
Find the total ounces in the 8-pack: \(6\times8=48\) oz for \(\$2.39\).

There are \(128\) oz in \(1\) gallon. Set up a proportion:

\[\dfrac{48\text{ oz}}{\$2.39}=\dfrac{128\text{ oz}}{x}\]
\[48x=\$2.39\times128=\$305.92\]
\[x=\$6.37\text{ per gallon}\]

questions.question:
A grocery store sells \(1\)-gallon containers of milk for $\(3.49\). The store also sells orange juice in a \(4\)-pack of \(8\)-fluid-ounce bottles for $\(2.99\). Suppose the store wants to sell its orange juice in gallon containers instead. To the nearest dollar, how much more would a gallon of orange juice cost than a gallon of milk?

Enter your answer in the space.

solution.exhibit_text:
Find the total ounces in the 4-pack: \(8\times4=32\) oz for \(\$2.99\).

There are \(128\) oz in \(1\) gallon. Set up a proportion:

\[\dfrac{32\text{ oz}}{\$2.99}=\dfrac{128\text{ oz}}{x}\]
\[32x=\$2.99\times128=\$382.72\]
\[x=\$11.96\text{ per gallon}\]

Subtract the cost of milk: \(\$11.96-\$3.49=\$8.47\), which rounds to \(\$8\).

questions.question:
I. \(p-q\)
II. \(pq^2\)
III. \(p^q\)

If \(p\) is a positive integer and \(q\) is a negative integer, which of the above expressions **must** be a positive number?

solution.exhibit_text:
I. \(p-q\): subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive, so \(p-q=p+|q|\), which is always positive.

II. \(pq^2\): squaring the negative \(q\) gives a positive number, and a positive times a positive is positive.

III. \(p^q\): a positive base raised to a negative power gives \(\dfrac{1}{p^{|q|}}\), which is still positive.

All three expressions must be positive.

questions.question: What is the value of \(\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right)\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
The product of two negative values is positive:

\[\dfrac{(-2)\times(-3)}{3\times7}=\dfrac{6}{21}\]

Simplify: \(\dfrac{6\div3}{21\div3}=\dfrac{2}{7}\).

questions.question: What is the value of \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{6}\right)\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
The product of two negative values is positive:

\[\dfrac{(-5)\times(-1)}{6\times4}=\dfrac{5}{24}\]

This fraction cannot be simplified further, so the answer is \(\dfrac{5}{24}\).

questions.question: What is the value of \(\left(-\dfrac{4}{9}\right)\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
The product of two negative values is positive:

\[\dfrac{(-4)\times(-3)}{9\times5}=\dfrac{12}{45}\]

Simplify: \(\dfrac{12\div3}{45\div3}=\dfrac{4}{15}\).
